{{Short description|Officials in ancient Japan during the Yamato period}}
{{Nihongo|'''''Kuni no miyatsuko'''''|国造|}}, also read as '''''kokuzō''''' or '''''kunitsuko''''', were officials in [[:en:Ancient Japan|Ancient Japan]] during the {{ill|Yamato period|ar|فترة ياماتو|be|Ямата (перыяд)|bg|Ямато (период)|ca|Període Yamato|ckb|سەردەمی یەماتۆ|cs|Období Jamato|de|Yamato-Zeit|eo|Epoko de Jamato|es|Período Yamato|fa|دوره یاماتو|fi|Yamato-kausi|fr|Période Yamato|hr|Yamato (razdoblje)|hu|Jamato-kor|id|Zaman Yamato|it|Periodo Yamato|ja|大和時代|ko|야마토 시대|ms|Zaman Yamato|nl|Yamatoperiode|pl|Yamato (okres)|ps|ياماتو|pt|Período Yamato|ro|Perioada Yamato|ru|Период Ямато|sh|Yamato period|sq|Periudha Jamato|sr|Јамато (период)|sv|Yamato (tidsperiod)|tl|Panahong Yamato|tr|Yamato Dönemi|uk|Період Ямато|vi|Thời kỳ Yamato|zh|大和時代|zh_min_nan|Yamato sî-tāi|qid=Q633881|lt=Yamato period}} who governed provinces called ''kuni''.

==Yamato period==

''Kuni no miyatsuko'' governed provinces called ''kuni'' (国), although the location, names, and borders of the provinces remain unclear. ''Kuni no miyatsuko'' were appointed by and remained under the jurisdiction of the Yamato Court, but over time the position became hereditary.<ref name="dijitaru">{{cite encyclopedia|encyclopedia=Dijitaru daijisen |title=国造 (Kuni no miyatsuko) |url=http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ |accessdate=2012-04-12 |year=2012 |publisher=Shogakukan |location=Tokyo |language=ja |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070825113418/http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ |archivedate=2007-08-25 }}</ref><ref name="encyclopedia">{{cite encyclopedia|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Japan |title=Kuni no miyatsuko |url=http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ |accessdate=2012-04-12 |year=2012 |publisher=Shogakukan |location=Tokyo |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070825113418/http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ |archivedate=2007-08-25 }}</ref> ''Kuni no miyatsuko'' carried ''[[kabane]]'' titles bestowed by the Yamato Court, commonly [[Kimi (kabane)|''kimi'']] (君) or ''[[atae]]'' (直). Prestigious ''kuni no miyatsuko'' held the title of ''[[Omi (title)|omi]]'' (臣).<ref name="encyclopedia"/>

==Taika Reforms==

The office of ''kuni no miyatsuko'' was abolished in the [[Taika Reform]]s in 645 and the former administrative ''kuni'' (provinces) were formally reorganized under the ''[[Ritsuryō]]'' system. The provinces became ruled by new officials called ''kuni no mikotomochi'', or more commonly, {{ill|Kokushi (official)|az|Kokuşi (vəzifə)|de|Kokushi|es|Kokushi|fa|کوکوشی|ff|Kokushi (official)|fr|Kokushi|it|Kokushi (ufficiale)|ja|国司|ko|고쿠시|pt|Kokushi|ru|Кокуси|sr|Кокуши|uk|Кокусі|vi|Kokushi|zh|國司|qid=Q1351234|lt=''kokushi''}}.<ref name="encyclopedia"/> The ''kuni no miyatsuko'' continued to be appointed after the Taika Reforms, generally to the office of {{Nihongo|gunji|郡司|}}.<ref name="dijitaru"/> ''Gunji'' were appointed from powerful regional ''kuni no miyatsuko'' families, for life, and the position became hereditary.<ref name="dijitaru-gunji">{{cite encyclopedia|encyclopedia=Dijitaru daijisen |title=郡司 (Gunji) |url=http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ |accessdate=2012-04-12 |year=2012 |publisher=Shogakukan |location=Tokyo |language=ja |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070825113418/http://rekishi.jkn21.com/ |archivedate=2007-08-25 }}</ref> The ''kuni no miyatsuko'' were now in charge of spiritual and religious affairs, specifically the [[Shinto|Shintō]] rites of each province.<ref name="encyclopedia"/> These religious officials became known as {{Nihongo|shin-kokuzō|新国造|}}, or "new" ''kuni no miyatsuko''.<ref name="encyclopedia"/> The ''kuni no miyatsuko'', now in the office of ''gunji'', often sided with peasants against the ruling ''kokushi'' elite. The ''gunji'' position, however, was abolished with the establishment of the manorial ''[[shōen]]'' system in the early {{ill|Heian period|ar|فترة هييآن|ast|Periodu Heian|az|Heyan dövrü|bcl|Panahon ni == Legacy ==
After their abolition several former Kuni no Miyatsuko became prominent priestly families these include the [[Izumo clan]] of [[Izumo-taisha]], the [[Aso clan]] of [[Aso Shrine]], the [[Owari clan]] of [[:en:Atsuta Jingu|Atsuta Jingu]], the {{ill|Munakata clan|fr|Clan Munakata|ja|宗像氏|simple|Munakata clan|qid=Q16481907}} of [[Munakata Taisha]],<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Matsunaga |first=Naomichi |title=Kuni no miyatsuko |url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=8839 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://archive.today/20231025020641/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=8839 |archive-date=2023-10-25 |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Kokugakuin University Encyclopedia of Shinto |language=en}}</ref> the [[Amabe clan]] of [[Kono Shrine]]<ref name="Bunka1">{{cite web |title=海部氏系図 |trans-title=Amebe shikeizu |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/201/777 |accessdate=August 20, 2020 |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |language=Japanese}}</ref> and the [[Yamato no Kuni no Miyatsuko|Yamato clan]] of [[Ōyamato Shrine]].
